title: How to lead a happy life (The Educated Barbarian: Seneca analysis, part. 1)
summary: First Educated Barbarian episode on Seneca's On the Happy Life, closing the Stoicism cycle after Marcus Aurelius (poetic) and Epictetus (theory). NH reads chapters 1-2: happiness is subjective but reached by reason, a sound mind and wisdom; leave the crowd, love yourself, apply philosophy rather than just talk about it, and feel emotions without being ruled by them.
claims: He's dropping Epictetus's Discourses and moving next to Nietzsche, Jung and related books
Reading order for Stoicism: Marcus Aurelius first for warmth, then Epictetus for theory, then Seneca for practice
What makes one person happy would make another miserable; only you can lead yourself to a happy life
Progress toward happiness, like lifting, is slow and noticed in hindsight as an epiphany
Follow your own reason rather than any guru, including him
The majority is often wrong; mistakes spread like a virus through groups
Leave the crowd mentally; letting a collective think for you makes you a puppet
People follow others because failure then isn't their fault; that comfort must be rejected
Self-improvement gurus selling happiness formulas are false prophets since the means is already within you
Depending on others for happiness gives you an excuse and almost guarantees failure; rely on yourself
A sound mind, not body or wealth, is the condition for happiness; the journey itself is the happy life
Joy is serene and sober; modern pursuit of money, casual sex and consumption is immediate gratification, not happiness
Seneca treats the body as unavoidable, not to be ignored but bent to the mind; comfort is vain
Wisdom is the key to happiness but useless unless applied; philosophy is an applied science
Modern philosophers who don't live their philosophy are posers; ancient philosophers were physically active men
Events have no inherent meaning; how you take them is within your control
Rigid principles are needed; modern relativism produces people with no spine
Your true self is found on the path, not before it; people who keep reinventing themselves are dodging the work
Self-love is the first step to the happy life; self-hatred locks the path
Nothing outside is trying to stop your happiness; only you can block yourself
Stoicism is not feeling nothing; it is feeling emotion and controlling it, and virtue requires temptation
Be wary of people who claim to have no dark thoughts: they're deceiving you or unaware of their own demons
Wisdom has degrees but it's not a competition; even the wisest still have flaws
